title: Chicago audition, Jack Tebo and rehearsals with Forest Hardy
summary: At the Fine Arts Building a booker, Jack Tebo, wires him to join a Chautauqua act; scared because he cannot read fast, he goes and quickly fits in under leader Forest Hardy.

story.theme_name: Chicago: the jazz migration and its clubs
story.community_name: Going north: working the Chicago jazz scene

blocks.x: -- so I went up and we -- everyday we had two or three auditions, we'd just take them --I had two
cases and I'd go in with them and sit with them and set up and here we'd go. So we were in the Fine Arts Building in Chicago and --
Uh -- you went to Chicago?
Yeah, we went up to Chat -- that's where we did our auditions.
Oh.

And it was in the Spring, I think around April. Or May, around the first of May. And we'd do an audition for the people in the Fine Arts Building. Ah, it was -- wait a minute, what was the name of that girl. Anyway the guy's name was Jack Tebo who came to me, I remember his name, and he said, (unintelligible) going off in the summer, Chattanooga; the fellow had to be operated on. We need somebody and I can't find anybody. He said, 'You'll be perfect.' I said, 'But I can't read, I don't know' -- He said, 'You'll learn the thing, they all played, it'll be simple for you.' I said, 'No. I can't.' I was scared to death. I didn't even know how to talk to him.
Weren't you kind of thrilled though?
No, I wasn't thrilled at all. Actually, I wasn't thrilled at all.
You were frightened?
Yes, I knew -- the idea was thrilling --
Yeah.
To think that I -- the idea to do it, but
Yeah.
-- I wasn't -- wasn't --
Yeah, capable.

No. I wasn't capable. So he kept wiring me to come. That he wanted me there. So I was graduating from high school. In May. So my mother said to me, "Look. It's still the same thing; in September you're going to go to Champaign, go to the University of Illinois. So what have you got to lose, all he can do is send you home? You can travel for nothing to Chicago. And she said if you make it, you might enjoy it. In the summer.
Yeah, yeah.
And so I was a little scared, but finally I thought, well, if he's insistent -- if he's willing to take a chance, I am too.
It's not your fault, then.
So she's right, all they can do is send me home.
Well.
So I went up and we had a week of rehearsals, and I caught onto it and we were all playing different parts. And I suddenly realized that I could fit in, I knew I could do it.
Yeah.
I knew that it would take time, but I knew I could do it and the lead man, by the name of Forest Hardy, was a drummer and a xylophone player -- he was very encouraging.
Oh.

He said, 'You got great hands. You got great hands, it'll be no problem for you.' I said, 'What do you mean?' He said, 'Well I don't know you don't play it like a drummer or anything.' He said, 'You got good hands on it.' He said, 'In another week you'll have it all down.'
